labels.3: Positive behaviours present but narrow or mixed
labels.5: Varied positive behaviours across the session

competencies.name: Communicating clearly
competencies.definition: Expresses ideas, information and reasoning so that others in the group can understand and use them, adapting to the audience.

indicators.text: States the point first, then supports it
examples: In short, what I'm proposing is

indicators.text: Structures a longer contribution explicitly by signposting or enumerating
examples: There are two options: first, second

indicators.text: Explains a term or gives an example when others signal confusion
examples: Let me put that differently
For example

indicators.text: Summarises own position concisely when asked
Checks that the message was understood
examples: Does that make sense?

indicators.text: Closes the loop on a request: confirms what was heard and what will be done
examples: So you need it by Friday, I'll send it Thursday

indicators.text: Gives a long, unstructured turn after which others ask what was meant
Uses unexplained jargon and does not clarify when asked
Repeatedly restarts or contradicts own statements without resolving them
Leaves a direct question unanswered

anchors.1: Contributions are hard to follow and are not repaired when others ask; direct questions stay unanswered.
anchors.3: Usually understandable, but structure, examples or checks appear only occasionally or only when asked.
anchors.5: Leads with the point, structures longer contributions, clarifies on confusion and closes the loop, across the session.

sources: SHL Great Eight: Interacting and Presenting
UK Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing
SHRM BASK: Communication
LifeComp: S2 Communication
Assessment-centre dimension: Communication (Arthur et al. 2003)
Salas, Sims & Burke 2005: closed-loop communication
competencies.limits: Vocal delivery, pace and prosody; visual aids; written communication; whether the content was correct. Do not use disfluencies, grammar or accent.

competencies.name: Active listening and uptake
competencies.definition: Attends to what others say and demonstrably uses it: paraphrases, asks follow-up questions and builds on others' contributions.

indicators.text: Paraphrases or summarises another speaker before responding
examples: If I understood you, you're saying

indicators.text: Asks a follow-up question that depends on the content of the previous turn
examples: What did you mean by

indicators.text: Explicitly builds on a named colleague's idea
examples: Building on what Ana said

indicators.text: Refers back to something said earlier by someone else
examples: Going back to Luis's point about

indicators.text: Asks a clarifying question instead of assuming
examples: Where does that number come from?

indicators.text: Corrects own understanding after an answer
examples: Ah, I had understood something else

indicators.text: Responds with an unrelated point right after a direct contribution
Repeats a proposal someone else already made without acknowledging it
Asks for information that was just given
Cuts in to finish another's sentence with a different meaning, and the speaker has to repair it

anchors.1: Responds beside the point, repeats others' proposals without acknowledging them or asks for what was just said.
anchors.3: Responds to others' content, but rarely paraphrases, asks follow-up questions or builds on it.
anchors.5: Paraphrases, asks content-dependent questions and builds on named colleagues' ideas throughout the session.

sources: UK Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; Working Together
OECD Competency Framework: Diplomatic Sensitivity
SHRM BASK: Communication (listening)
LifeComp: S1 Empathy; S2 Communication
PISA 2015 CPS: Establishing and maintaining shared understanding
CATME: Interacting with teammates
SHL Great Eight: Supporting and Cooperating
competencies.limits: Silent attention, eye contact, note-taking; whether the understanding was real. Do not score back-channels ("mm-hm"): transcription drops them and they vary by culture.

competencies.name: Influencing with reasons
competencies.definition: Gains others' agreement through evidence, argument and appeal to shared goals, while remaining open to counter-argument.

indicators.text: Gives a reason, a fact or an example together with a proposal
examples: I'd go with B because

indicators.text: Links the proposal to a goal the group has stated
examples: Given we agreed the priority is

indicators.text: Anticipates and addresses an objection
Adjusts the proposal after a counter-argument and says so
examples: You're right about the cost; what if we

indicators.text: Proposes a trade-off or package that incorporates others' interests
Asks what others would need in order to agree
examples: What would convince you?

indicators.text: Repeats the same assertion without new support
Appeals to status, seniority or experience instead of reasons
examples: I have been doing this for years

indicators.text: Pushes for closure while objections are unanswered
examples: There is nothing more to discuss

indicators.text: Dismisses alternatives without engaging with their content

anchors.1: Pushes by repetition, status or pressure to close; dismisses alternatives without engaging with them.
anchors.3: Gives reasons for proposals, but rarely links them to shared goals or responds to objections.
anchors.5: Argues with reasons tied to the group's goals, addresses objections and adjusts the proposal in response.

sources: SHL Great Eight: Interacting and Presenting; Leading and Deciding
UK Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing
OECD Competency Framework: Influencing; Negotiating
SHRM BASK: Relationship Management (negotiation)
Assessment-centre dimension: Influencing others (Arthur et al. 2003)
competencies.limits: Whether minds changed beyond the meeting; lobbying outside it; the quality of the evidence cited; whether the group's choice was good. A proposal being adopted is NOT evidence: it rewards status and talk time.

competencies.name: Collaboration and mutual support
competencies.definition: Works toward shared goals: offers and asks for help, shares information, credits others and puts the team result ahead of personal position.

indicators.text: Offers concrete help with a teammate's task
examples: I can take that off your plate

indicators.text: Asks for help or input when stuck
examples: Could someone look at this with me?

indicators.text: Shares, unprompted, information that another member needs
examples: You'll need the figures I got, I'll share them

indicators.text: Credits a named colleague for an idea or for work done
examples: That was Marta's idea

indicators.text: Frames goals and problems collectively
examples: What do we need

indicators.text: Volunteers for an unglamorous shared task
Withholds or deflects when asked for information
examples: That's my part, don't worry about it

indicators.text: Disparages a teammate's contribution or competence
examples: That makes no sense at all

indicators.text: Claims shared work as own
Refuses a reasonable request for help without explanation

anchors.1: Withholds information or help, disparages teammates or claims shared work as own.
anchors.3: Cooperates when asked, but rarely offers help, shares information unprompted or credits others.
anchors.5: Offers and asks for help, shares what others need and credits colleagues, repeatedly and unprompted.

sources: SHL Great Eight: Supporting and Cooperating
UK Success Profiles: Working Together
OECD Competency Framework: Teamwork and Team Leadership
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Connect and Collaborate
SHRM BASK: Relationship Management (teamwork)
LifeComp: S3 Collaboration
Salas, Sims & Burke 2005: backup behaviour; team orientation
Marks, Mathieu & Zaccaro 2001: team monitoring and backup
CATME: Interacting with teammates
Stevens & Campion 1994: interpersonal KSAs
competencies.limits: Whether the help offered was delivered; the amount and quality of the work actually contributed; trust; behaviour outside the recorded session.

competencies.name: Inclusive facilitation
competencies.definition: Helps everyone contribute: invites quieter members, balances airtime, protects speakers from being talked over and makes room for different viewpoints.

indicators.text: Directly invites a member who has not spoken on the topic
examples: Carlos, we haven't heard from you on this

indicators.text: Returns the floor to someone who was cut off
examples: Hang on, Lucía was saying

indicators.text: Asks for dissenting or missing views before closing a topic
examples: Does anyone see it differently?

indicators.text: Checks the whole group for agreement instead of assuming it
examples: Is everyone OK with that, or just the three of us?

indicators.text: Limits own turn to make room for others
examples: I've talked a lot, what do others think?

indicators.text: Rephrases a hesitant contribution so the group considers it
Talks over a member who is starting to speak, and that member gives up the turn
Addresses questions only to the same one or two members
Declares consensus when others have not spoken
examples: So we all agree

indicators.text: Dismisses a contribution by referring to who said it

anchors.1: Talks over others, addresses only the same one or two members or declares agreement nobody voiced.
anchors.3: Leaves room for others, but seldom invites, protects a speaker or checks the whole group.
anchors.5: Invites quiet members, returns the floor to interrupted speakers and asks for dissent before closing, throughout.

sources: UK Success Profiles: Working Together; Leadership
OECD Competency Framework: Teamwork and Team Leadership
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Inclusion; Connect and Collaborate
ATC21S: Participation; Social regulation
PISA 2015 CPS: Establishing and maintaining team organisation
Salas, Sims & Burke 2005: team leadership
Woolley et al. 2010: equality of conversational turn-taking
competencies.limits: The intent behind overlapping speech (often cooperative, especially in Spanish); gaze and gesture; whether someone's silence is exclusion or choice. Talking-over evidence is low confidence when timing or speaker labels are unreliable.

competencies.name: Constructive disagreement and conflict handling
competencies.definition: Raises and handles disagreement about tasks and ideas openly and respectfully, separates issues from persons and works toward resolution.

indicators.text: States disagreement explicitly with a reason
examples: I see it differently, because

indicators.text: Acknowledges the valid part of the other view before differing
examples: I agree on the goal, not on the timing

indicators.text: Names the disagreement and proposes a way to resolve it: criteria, data, a test or a vote
examples: Can we agree how to decide?

indicators.text: Reframes a personal remark as an issue about the task
Proposes a compromise or an option that integrates both views
examples: We could combine both options

indicators.text: De-escalates after tension: apologises or takes back wording
examples: Sorry, that came out harsher than I meant

indicators.text: Makes a personal criticism or a sarcastic remark aimed at a member
Rejects an idea outright without giving reasons
examples: That will never work

indicators.text: Complains repeatedly without proposing anything
Explicitly withdraws after a disagreement
examples: Fine, do whatever you want

anchors.1: Disagrees through personal criticism, blanket rejection or withdrawal.
anchors.3: States disagreement with reasons, but seldom acknowledges the other view or proposes how to resolve it.
anchors.5: Disagrees with reasons, acknowledges the other view, proposes a way to decide or a compromise and de-escalates tension.

sources: Stevens & Campion 1994: conflict resolution KSAs
Marks, Mathieu & Zaccaro 2001: conflict management; affect management
OECD Competency Framework: Teamwork and Team Leadership; Diplomatic Sensitivity; Negotiating
UK Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing; Making Effective Decisions
SHRM BASK: Relationship Management (conflict management)
LifeComp: S3 Collaboration; P1 Self-regulation
ATC21S: Social regulation
competencies.limits: Emotional state, tone and sarcasm; disagreement that was not voiced; conflict history outside the recording. A session without disagreement gives no evidence: insufficient evidence, not a high rating. Do not score politeness formulas or hedging.

competencies.name: Feedback and developing others
competencies.definition: Gives specific, usable feedback, asks for feedback on own work, and explains and teaches so that others can do the task.

indicators.text: Gives feedback that names the specific behaviour or piece of work and its effect
examples: The intro works; the second section loses me at

indicators.text: Pairs a criticism with a concrete suggestion
examples: Maybe move that part to the end

indicators.text: Asks for feedback on own contribution
examples: Can you tell me what you'd change in my part?

indicators.text: Explains how or why, not only what, when a teammate lacks knowledge
examples: The reason we do it this way is

indicators.text: Checks whether the explanation helped
examples: Is that clearer now?

indicators.text: Recognises improvement or good work specifically
examples: Nice work on the edge cases

indicators.text: Gives a global judgement without specifics
examples: This is bad

indicators.text: Takes over a teammate's task instead of explaining, after being asked for help to learn
Rejects or argues with feedback received without considering it
Delivers feedback as a put-down in front of the group

anchors.1: Judges globally without specifics, puts teammates down or rejects feedback received.
anchors.3: Gives feedback or explanations when asked, with limited specifics; seldom asks for feedback.
anchors.5: Gives specific feedback with suggestions, explains the why, checks it helped and asks for feedback on own work.

sources: UK Success Profiles: Developing Self and Others
OECD Competency Framework: Developing Talent
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Learn and Develop
CATME: Keeping the team on track; Expecting quality
Salas, Sims & Burke 2005: mutual performance monitoring
Marks, Mathieu & Zaccaro 2001: team monitoring and backup
Edmondson 1999: team learning behaviours
competencies.limits: Whether the feedback was accurate; whether the recipient improved; private or written feedback. Many sessions contain no feedback episode: expect insufficient evidence often.

competencies.name: Coordination and keeping the team on track
competencies.definition: Structures the group's work: clarifies goals, proposes process, allocates tasks and time, monitors progress and summarises.

indicators.text: States or asks for the goal or output of the session
examples: What do we need to have decided by the end?

indicators.text: Proposes an agenda, an order or a method
examples: Let's do requirements first, then split tasks

indicators.text: Proposes or negotiates who does what by when
examples: Pablo the draft by Wednesday, I review Thursday

indicators.text: Notes the time and redirects the group
examples: Ten minutes left; let's decide this first

indicators.text: Summarises decisions and open points
examples: To sum up, we agreed that

indicators.text: Brings the discussion back after a digression
examples: We're drifting, back to the budget

indicators.text: Repeatedly introduces unrelated topics while a task is open
Reopens settled decisions without new information
Leaves task ownership ambiguous when asked
examples: Someone will do it

indicators.text: Dictates assignments without checking capacity or agreement

anchors.1: Derails or reopens settled points, leaves ownership vague or dictates assignments without checking.
anchors.3: Follows the structure others set and occasionally proposes a step, an owner or a deadline.
anchors.5: Sets goals and method, negotiates who does what by when, watches the time and summarises decisions and open points.

sources: Marks, Mathieu & Zaccaro 2001: transition processes (goal specification, planning); action processes (monitoring progress, coordination)
Stevens & Campion 1994: goal setting; planning and task coordination
CATME: Keeping the team on track
SHL Great Eight: Organizing and Executing
Assessment-centre dimension: Organising and planning (Arthur et al. 2003)
UK Success Profiles: Delivering at Pace; Leadership
OECD Competency Framework: Teamwork and Team Leadership; Managing Resources
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Analyse and Plan
PISA 2015 CPS: Establishing and maintaining team organisation
ATC21S: Task regulation
competencies.limits: Whether the plans were realistic or carried out; coordination done in tools (boards, chat). A designated facilitator showing these behaviours is fulfilling a role: the report must say so.

competencies.name: Collaborative problem solving and decision making
competencies.definition: Contributes to analysing problems and reaching decisions with the group: defines the problem, shares and requests relevant information, generates and evaluates options and makes the reasoning explicit.

indicators.text: Defines or reframes the problem; separates symptom from cause
examples: What exactly is the problem we're solving?

indicators.text: Asks for facts or assumptions before judging an option
examples: Do we know that, or are we assuming it?

indicators.text: Offers more than one option, or asks for alternatives
States criteria and weighs the options against them
examples: Option A is cheaper but riskier because

indicators.text: Makes the chain of reasoning explicit
examples: If we do this, then

indicators.text: Checks the decision against the goal and names remaining risks
examples: What would have to be true for this to fail?

indicators.text: Jumps to a solution and resists examining the problem
examples: I know what the solution is, let's just do it

indicators.text: Asserts conclusions with no stated basis when challenged
Ignores disconfirming information raised by others
Pushes to decide without stating what is being decided

anchors.1: Jumps to a solution, asserts without basis when challenged or ignores information that contradicts it.
anchors.3: Contributes facts and opinions, but seldom frames the problem, compares options or states criteria.
anchors.5: Defines the problem, checks facts and assumptions, weighs options against criteria and tests the decision against the goal.

sources: PISA 2015 CPS: Taking appropriate action to solve the problem; Establishing and maintaining shared understanding
ATC21S: Task regulation; Knowledge building
Stevens & Campion 1994: collaborative problem solving KSAs
UK Success Profiles: Making Effective Decisions
OECD Competency Framework: Analytical Thinking; Flexible Thinking
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Analyse and Plan
SHL Great Eight: Analyzing and Interpreting; Leading and Deciding
Assessment-centre dimension: Problem solving (Arthur et al. 2003)
competencies.limits: Whether the analysis was correct, technical expertise, thinking done silently or in writing, and the quality of the decision. The rubric rates the contribution to the process, not being right.

competencies.name: Initiative and commitment to action
competencies.definition: Moves the work forward: volunteers, proposes next steps, commits to concrete actions and reports on earlier commitments.

indicators.text: Volunteers for a task with a concrete deliverable or date
examples: I'll take it, you'll have it Monday

indicators.text: Proposes a next step when the group stalls
examples: Next step: I'll call the client today

indicators.text: Reports the status of an earlier commitment without being asked
Admits a missed or at-risk commitment and re-plans
examples: I didn't finish the analysis; I'll have it tomorrow morning

indicators.text: Raises the quality bar with a specific standard
examples: Let's test it with two users first

indicators.text: Expresses confidence in the team's ability to deliver, tied to a plan
Deflects responsibility
examples: Not my job
Nobody told me

indicators.text: Gives a vague non-commitment when asked directly
examples: I'll see

indicators.text: Is pessimistic about any change without offering an alternative
examples: There's no point

indicators.text: Acknowledges repeated non-delivery without explanation

anchors.1: Deflects responsibility, stays vague when asked to commit or is pessimistic without alternatives.
anchors.3: Accepts tasks when they are assigned; commitments are sometimes concrete, rarely volunteered.
anchors.5: Volunteers with deliverables and dates, proposes next steps, reports status and re-plans openly when something slips.

sources: CATME: Contributing to the team's work; Expecting quality
Assessment-centre dimension: Drive (Arthur et al. 2003; Meriac et al. 2014)
SHL Great Eight: Enterprising and Performing; Organizing and Executing
UK Success Profiles: Delivering at Pace
OECD Competency Framework: Achievement Focus
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Deliver Results with Positive Impact
Marks, Mathieu & Zaccaro 2001: motivating and confidence building
Kauffeld & Lehmann-Willenbrock 2012 (act4teams): action-oriented statements
competencies.limits: Follow-through: a transcript shows commitments, not delivery. Effort, working hours and the quality of the output are not observable. Delivery can only be seen by linking sessions.

competencies.name: Openness to learning and adaptability
competencies.definition: Shows willingness to revise views and approach: admits gaps and mistakes, asks for help, incorporates new information and adjusts to changed constraints.

indicators.text: Says "I don't know" or "I was wrong" in plain terms
examples: My mistake: I used last year's data
Honestly, I don't know

indicators.text: Changes position after an argument or new information and says why
examples: Good point, I hadn't considered that; then I'd change

indicators.text: Asks how someone else would approach it
examples: How would you do it?

indicators.text: Proposes adjusting the plan when a constraint changes
examples: What if we change the plan and do it in two phases?

indicators.text: Reflects on what the team could do differently next time
examples: Next time we should start with

indicators.text: Accepts feedback and states what will change
Defends a position after it has been factually corrected
Blames others or circumstances for an error raised in the session
Rejects a changed constraint without proposing how to cope
examples: We've always done it this way

indicators.text: Dismisses a retrospective or feedback discussion as a waste of time

anchors.1: Defends positions after being corrected, blames others or rejects change and feedback.
anchors.3: Accepts corrections and new constraints, but seldom says what changed or asks how others would do it.
anchors.5: Admits gaps and mistakes plainly, changes position with reasons, adapts the plan and reflects on what to do differently.

sources: Edmondson 1999: team learning behaviours
Salas, Sims & Burke 2005: adaptability
SHL Great Eight: Adapting and Coping
OECD Competency Framework: Flexible Thinking
UK Success Profiles: Changing and Improving; Developing Self and Others
UN Values and Behaviours Framework: Adapt and Innovate; Learn and Develop; Humility
LifeComp: P2 Flexibility; L1 Growth mindset
ATC21S: Social regulation
competencies.limits: Actual learning or later behaviour change; private reflection; resilience or stress tolerance. Admitting errors depends on the team climate: few admissions may reflect the team, not the person.

excluded.name: Integrity, honesty, ethics
excluded.reason: Needs knowledge of facts and of behaviour when unobserved; a transcript only shows claims.

excluded.name: Technical expertise; correctness of ideas
excluded.reason: Needs domain ground truth and work products.

excluded.name: Reliability, work quality, follow-through
excluded.reason: Happen outside the conversation; only commitments are audible.

excluded.name: Results orientation
excluded.reason: An outcome construct, not a conversational behaviour.

excluded.name: Strategic thinking, vision
excluded.reason: Not sampled in peer work sessions; inference would rest on vocabulary.

excluded.name: Emotional intelligence, emotional state, stress tolerance
excluded.reason: Internal states; text is a poor proxy, and inferring emotion from voice at work or in education is prohibited by the EU AI Act.

excluded.name: Psychological safety, trust, cohesion
excluded.reason: Shared beliefs of the team, measured by survey.

excluded.name: Personality, Belbin roles, MBTI or DISC types, motivation
excluded.reason: Dispositional constructs; the instruments have weak psychometric support and automated inference weak validity.

excluded.name: Cognitive ability
excluded.reason: Not a behavioural competency; verbal fluency is a biased proxy.

excluded.name: Leadership as a separate score
excluded.reason: Emergent and shared in peer groups, and perceptions of it follow speaking time; reported as a profile of INCL, COORD, INFLU, FEEDB and INIT evidence.
